Analytical notes, supporting results, and response material for the eLife revision.

**Goal**: compare a covariance-dominated rule with the rate-dominated rule in a setting with multiple competing inhibitory-to-excitatory connections.

Throughout, we take $h_e>0$, $r_i>0$, and all kernel timescales positive. We assume $M>0$ for both rules; for the covariance-dominated rule, this requires $\tau_->\tau_+$. The inputs, inhibitory rate, fixed weight $W_e$, and rule constants are held constant during the weight dynamics.

## Three neuron motif {#sec-three-neuron-motif}

![Three-neuron motif with one excitatory neuron and two inhibitory neurons. The diagram labels the excitatory input $h_e$, an excitatory-to-inhibitory connection $W_e$, two inhibitory-to-excitatory connections $W_1$ and $W_2$, inhibitory rates are $r_i$, fixed by an adaptive input.](Attachments/20261005-113251-three_neurons_motif.png){#fig-three-neuron-motif fig-alt="c_1 cyan triangular neuron above two magenta circular neurons. Blue arrows indicate input and an excitatory connection; red dashed connections with terminal dots link both lower neurons to the upper neuron." width=450px}

We consider a simple three-neuron motif, with one excitatory neuron and two inhibitory neurons, modeled as Hawkes processes (@fig-three-neuron-motif). The excitatory neuron receives a constant input $h_e$, and projects to one of the inhibitory neurons with a strong weight $W_e$. The two inhibitory neurons project back to the excitatory neuron with plastic weights $W_1$ and $W_2$. All neurons have an exponential synaptic kernel with timescale $\tau_{\text{syn}}$.

In the three-neuron system of @fig-three-neuron-motif, the inhibitory rates $r_i$ are kept constant by an adaptive input. The excitatory rate instead is given by:
$$
r_e = h_e - W_1 \,r_i - W_2 \,r_i = h_e - (W_1 + W_2) \,r_i
$$ {#eq-excitatory-rate}

The excitatory neuron projects to a single inhibitory neuron with a fixed weight $W_e$, that we assume strong. Therefore inhibitory neuron 1 will have a strong correlation with the excitatory neuron, while inhibitory neuron 2 will be assumed as uncorrelated.

The two inhibitory-to-excitatory weights $W_1$ and $W_2$ are plastic, following identical symmetric plasticity rules. The average synaptic weight dynamics are given by:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\,W_1}{dt} &= \alpha_{\text{pre}} \,r_i + \alpha_{\text{post}} \,r_e + B \,r_i \,r_e - M^{10}\,W_1\,r_i  + M^{01}\, W_e \, r_e \\
\frac{d\,W_2}{dt} &= \alpha_{\text{pre}} \,r_i + \alpha_{\text{post}} \,r_e + B \,r_i \,r_e - M^{10}\,W_2\,r_i
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-weight-dynamics}
Where $B$ is the area under the STDP curve, and the $M$ terms represent the first-order motif contributions to plasticity (ignoring higher order contributions). Since here we only consider symmetric rules $M^{10} = M^{01} := M$.

Let $\eta>0$ be the learning constant multiplying the entire right-hand side of every weight equation. The dynamics and fixed-point derivations below display $\eta=1$ for readability; the deviation matrices, eigenvalues, and relaxation times include $\eta$ explicitly. Each rule may use its own $\eta$, held constant during learning. It rescales time without changing the fixed point. The presynaptic and postsynaptic constants are calibrated parameters, rather than fixed nominal values.


In the Vogels-Spreckeler rule we have:
$$
\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{Vog}} = 0, \quad B^{\text{Vog}} = 1
$$ {#eq-vogels-constants}
The $M^{\text{Vog}}$ term is:
$$
M^{\text{Vog}} = \frac{1}{2\,\left(\tau_+ + \tau_{\text{syn}} \right)}
$$ {#eq-vogels-motif}
And $\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{Vog}}$ is a free parameter set to ensure that the rate of the excitatory neuron is maintained at a target value $r_e^{\text{(target)}}$.

In the covariance-dominated rule instead:
$$
 \quad B^{\text{cov}} = 0  ,\quad
M^{\text{cov}} = \frac{1}{2\,\left(\tau_+ + \tau_{\text{syn}} \right)}
-  \frac{1}{2\,\left(\tau_- + \tau_{\text{syn}} \right)}
$$ {#eq-covariance-motif}
And both $\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{cov}}$ and $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{cov}}$ are free parameters that can be used to set the target rate. Here for simplicity we will set $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{cov}} = 0$, but all our results hold in the general case (see detailed analytic notes).

For $\tau_- \gg \tau_+$ and $\tau_- \gg \tau_{\text{syn}}$, $M^{\text{Vog}}$ and $M^{\text{cov}}$ are similar. The main difference between the rules is therefore in the $B^{\text{Vog}}=1$ and $B^{\text{cov}}=0$ terms.

### Sum and difference modes {#sec-sum-difference-modes}

Keeping the rule constants general, we define the sum and difference modes as

$$
W_s := W_1 + W_2, \qquad W_d := W_1 - W_2.
$$ {#eq-weight-modes}

With this convention, $W_d > 0$ means that $W_1$ is stronger than $W_2$. The original weights are recovered as

$$
W_1 = \frac{W_s + W_d}{2}, \qquad
W_2 = \frac{W_s - W_d}{2}.
$$ {#eq-weight-modes-inverse}

Using @eq-excitatory-rate and the definition in @eq-weight-modes, the excitatory rate depends only on the sum mode:

$$
r_e = h_e - W_s\,r_i.
$$ {#eq-rate-sum-mode}

Adding and subtracting the two weight equations in @eq-weight-dynamics, with $M^{10} = M^{01} = M$, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\,W_s}{dt}
&= 2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i
 + 2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}\,r_e
 + 2\,B\,r_i\,r_e
 - M\,W_s\,r_i + M\,W_e\,r_e, \\
\frac{d\,W_d}{dt}
&= -M\,W_d\,r_i + M\,W_e\,r_e.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mode-dynamics}

Substituting @eq-rate-sum-mode yields a closed system for the two modes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\,W_s}{dt}
&= 2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i
 + \left(2\,\alpha_{\text{post}} + 2\,B\,r_i + M\,W_e\right)
   \left(h_e - W_s\,r_i\right)
 - M\,W_s\,r_i, \\
\frac{d\,W_d}{dt}
&= -M\,W_d\,r_i + M\,W_e\,\left(h_e - W_s\,r_i\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mode-dynamics-closed}

The shared rate-dependent plasticity terms cancel in the difference equation. The sum mode evolves independently of $W_d$, while the difference mode is driven by the sum through $r_e$ and by the additional $W_e$ term in the $W_1$ equation.

### Fixed points of the modes and individual weights {#sec-mode-fixed-points}

To simplify the expressions, define

$$
c_1 := 2\,\alpha_{\text{post}} + 2\,B\,r_i + M\,W_e,
\qquad c_2 := c_1 + M.
$$ {#eq-mode-coefficients}

Using @eq-mode-coefficients, the sum equation in @eq-mode-dynamics-closed becomes

$$
\frac{d\,W_s}{dt}
= 2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i + c_1\,h_e - r_i\,c_2\,W_s.
$$ {#eq-sum-affine}

Substituting $c_1$ and $c_2$ from @eq-mode-coefficients, the fixed point simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{M\,h_e - 2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i}
 {M\,(1+W_e) + 2\,\alpha_{\text{post}} + 2\,B\,r_i}, \\
W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{h_e-r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{r_i}
 = \frac{2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i
 + \left(2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+2\,B\,r_i+M\,W_e\right)\,h_e}
 {r_i\,\left[M\,(1+W_e)+2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+2\,B\,r_i\right]}, \\
W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{W_e\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{r_i}
 = \frac{W_e\,\left(M\,h_e-2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i\right)}
 {r_i\,\left[M\,(1+W_e)+2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+2\,B\,r_i\right]}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mode-fixed-points}

Recovering the individual weights with @eq-weight-modes-inverse gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
W_1^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}+W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{2}
 = \frac{h_e+(W_e-1)\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{2\,r_i} \\
&= \frac{\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,(1-W_e)\,r_i
 + \left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i+M\,W_e\right)\,h_e}
 {r_i\,\left[M\,(1+W_e)+2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+2\,B\,r_i\right]}, \\
W_2^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&= \frac{W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}-W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{2}
 = \frac{h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{2\,r_i} \\
&= \frac{\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,(1+W_e)\,r_i
 + \left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i\right)\,h_e}
 {r_i\,\left[M\,(1+W_e)+2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+2\,B\,r_i\right]}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-individual-weight-fixed-points}

These expressions assume a nonzero denominator; stability requires it to be positive, as shown below.

Thus, for $W_e > 0$ and $r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)} > 0$, the difference is positive: $W_1^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)} > W_2^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$. This follows from the additional excitatory-to-inhibitory motif contribution to the first weight.

These are algebraic fixed points of the unconstrained equations. For nonnegative inhibitory weight magnitudes and excitatory rate, they must also satisfy

$$
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)} \ge 0, \qquad W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)} \ge |W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}|.
$$ {#eq-mode-fixed-point-admissibility}

For $W_e \ge 0$, these conditions are equivalent to $0 \le r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)} \le h_e/(1+W_e)$. If they fail, the algebraic fixed point does not represent a state with nonnegative rates and weights; no weight clipping or boundary dynamics have been specified here.

#### Relative size of the difference and sum {#sec-fixed-point-mode-ratio}

For a stable fixed point with $W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}>0$ and $r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}>0$, the common denominator cancels in the ratio:

$$
\frac{W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}
= \frac{W_e\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{h_e-r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}
= \frac{W_e\,\left(M\,h_e-2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i\right)}
 {2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i
 + \left(2\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+2\,B\,r_i+M\,W_e\right)\,h_e}.
$$ {#eq-fixed-point-mode-ratio}

With strictly positive weights, the difference cannot be larger than the sum: $W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}-W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}=2\,W_2^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}>0$. For $W_e>0$, a physically admissible fixed point therefore has $0<W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}/W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}<1$. A ratio close to one means $W_2^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$ is small relative to $W_1^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$; equality means $W_2^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}=0$.

Setting the fixed-point rate equal to $r_e^{\text{(target)}}$ requires

$$
\alpha_{\text{pre}}
= -\frac{\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i}{r_i}\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}
 + \frac{M}{2\,r_i}\,
   \left[h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}\right].
$$ {#eq-report-target-presynaptic-constant}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Most important result here!

Given $h_e$, $r_i$, and $W_e$, the stable weights depend on the plasticity parameters only through $r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$. Therefore, if the parameters of each rule are chosen to produce the same target rate at a stable fixed point, the final inhibitory weights will also be the same across all possible rules considered here! The solution is rule-invariant, and the only difference between rules is in the dynamics of convergence to the fixed point!

:::


#### Vogels-Sprekeler rule {#sec-vogels-fixed-points}

With $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{Vog}}=0$ and $B^{\text{Vog}}=1$,

$$
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
= \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}\,h_e-2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i}
 {M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i},
\qquad
\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{Vog}}
= -r_e^{\text{(target)}}
 + \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}}{2\,r_i}\,
   \left[h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}\right].
$$ {#eq-report-vogels-target}


#### Covariance-based rule {#sec-covariance-fixed-points}

With $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{cov}}=0$ and $B^{\text{cov}}=0$, assuming
$M^{\text{cov}}>0$ (thus $\tau_->\tau_+$),

$$
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
= \frac{h_e}{1+W_e}
 - \frac{2\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{cov}}\,r_i}
 {M^{\text{cov}}\,(1+W_e)},
\qquad
\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{cov}}
= \frac{M^{\text{cov}}}{2\,r_i}\,
   \left[h_e-(1+W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}\right].
$$ {#eq-report-covariance-target}

### Convergence timescales of the sum and difference {#sec-mode-timescales}

The excitatory rate converges with the sum mode because $r_e=h_e-r_i\,W_s$. Reaching the target rate does not imply that the weight difference has settled.


Writing $\delta W_s := W_s-W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$ and $\delta W_d := W_d-W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$, the deviations obey the exact linear system

$$
\frac{d}{dt}
\begin{pmatrix}\delta W_s \\ \delta W_d\end{pmatrix}
=
\eta\,
\begin{pmatrix}
-r_i\,c_2 & 0 \\
-M\,W_e\,r_i & -M\,r_i
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\delta W_s \\ \delta W_d\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-mode-deviations}

The triangular matrix has eigenvalues $\lambda_s=-\eta\,r_i\,c_2$ and $\lambda_d=-\eta\,r_i\,M$. Therefore both modes converge to the algebraic fixed point precisely when $c_2>0$. Their exponential timescales are

$$
\tau_s = \frac{1}{\eta\,r_i\,c_2}, \qquad
\tau_d = \frac{1}{\eta\,r_i\,M}.
$$ {#eq-mode-timescales}

The ratio used in the report is

$$
\frac{\tau_s}{\tau_d}=\frac{M}{M\,(1+W_e)+2\,(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i)}.
$$ {#eq-mode-timescale-ratio}


The sum relaxes independently as $\delta W_s(t)=\delta W_s(0)\,e^{-t/\tau_s}$. The difference also receives a transient forcing from the sum, so its trajectory generally contains both timescales. Once the sum has settled, the difference relaxes toward $W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$ on $\tau_d$. When $c_2=M$, the forcing can produce a $t\,e^{-\eta\,M\,r_i\,t}$ transient. Special initial conditions can eliminate one of the exponential contributions.

The sum converges much faster than the difference when

$$
\frac{\tau_d}{\tau_s}
= \frac{c_2}{M}
= 1 + W_e + \frac{2\,\alpha_{\text{post}} + 2\,B\,r_i}{M}
\gg 1,
\qquad c_2>0.
$$ {#eq-mode-timescale-separation}

Thus a strong $W_e$, a sufficiently positive postsynaptic term, or a large positive rate-dependent term $B\,r_i$ can produce a fast sum and a slow difference. The presynaptic constant $\alpha_{\text{pre}}$ shifts the fixed point but does not change these eigenvalues. The inhibitory rate multiplies both decay rates and also affects their ratio through $B\,r_i$.

#### Vogels-Sprekeler rule {#sec-report-timescales-vogels}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}
&= \frac{1}
 {\eta^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i\,\left[M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i\right]}, \\
\tau_d^{\text{Vog}}
&= \frac{1}{\eta^{\text{Vog}}\,M^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i}.\\
\frac{\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}}{\tau_d^{\text{Vog}}}
&= \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}}
 {M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-report-vogels-timescale-ratio}

For $M^{\text{Vog}}\ll2\,r_i$, expanding gives

$$
\frac{\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}}{\tau_d^{\text{Vog}}}
= \frac{M^{\text{Vog}}}{2\,r_i}
 - \frac{(1+W_e)\,(M^{\text{Vog}})^2}{4\,r_i^2}
 + \mathcal{O}\!\left((M^{\text{Vog}})^3\right).
$$ {#eq-report-vogels-inverse-ratio-small-m}

Therefore $\tau_s \ll \tau_d$ , the sum relaxes much faster than the difference in this regime.

#### Covariance-based rule {#sec-report-timescales-covariance}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_s^{\text{cov}}
&= \frac{1}
 {\eta^{\text{cov}}\,M^{\text{cov}}\,r_i\,(1+W_e)}, \\
\tau_d^{\text{cov}}
&= \frac{1}{\eta^{\text{cov}}\,M^{\text{cov}}\,r_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-report-covariance-timescales}

$$
\frac{\tau_s^{\text{cov}}}{\tau_d^{\text{cov}}}
= \frac{1}{1+W_e}.
$$ {#eq-report-covariance-timescale-ratio}

This ratio is independent of $M^{\text{cov}}$ and in our parameter range $\mathcal{O}(1)$.

#### Matching the sum-mode timescales {#sec-report-matched-sum-timescales}

For the same $r_i$ and $W_e$, imposing
$\tau_s^{\text{Vog}}=\tau_s^{\text{cov}}$ requires

$$
\frac{\eta^{\text{Vog}}}{\eta^{\text{cov}}}
= \frac{M^{\text{cov}}\,(1+W_e)}
 {M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i}.
$$ {#eq-report-matched-learning-rates}

With nonnegative $\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i$ and $W_e>0$, $c_2>M$, so $\tau_s<\tau_d$: the difference mode is slower than the sum mode for both rules considered here. For the covariance rule with $\alpha_{\text{post}}=0$, the modes have comparable timescales when $W_e$ is of order one. A general nonzero postsynaptic constant is retained in @eq-mode-timescales and @eq-mode-timescale-separation.

For any prescribed common sum timescale $T>0$, choose

$$
\eta^{\text{Vog}}=\frac{1}{T\,r_i\,[M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+W_e)+2\,r_i]},
\qquad
\eta^{\text{cov}}=\frac{1}{T\,r_i\,M^{\text{cov}}\,(1+W_e)}.
$$ {#eq-common-sum-learning-rates}

The resulting difference timescales are $\tau_d^{\text{Vog}}=T\,[1+W_e+2\,r_i/M^{\text{Vog}}]$ and $\tau_d^{\text{cov}}=T\,(1+W_e)$. Matching the sum therefore leaves the Vogels difference mode slower. Learning rates rescale both modes together and do not change either rule's timescale ratio or calibrated fixed point.

## Generalization to N inhibitory neurons and K excitatory targets {#sec-n-k-generalization}

We now consider one excitatory neuron and $N$ inhibitory neurons, of which $K$ receive an excitatory-to-inhibitory synapse of fixed weight $W_e$ each (the $w_e$ in the generalized setup). Here

$$
N,K\in\mathbb{N}, \qquad 1\le K<N.
$$ {#eq-nk-domain}

Thus $N\ge2$, and both targeted and untargeted inhibitory groups are nonempty. The three-neuron motif above is the special case $N=2$, $K=1$. The weight $W_e\ge0$ is the weight of **each** excitatory synapse, so the total outgoing excitatory weight is $K\,W_e$.

We retain the same modeling assumptions: all inhibitory rates are held at the common value $r_i>0$ by adaptive inputs, all inhibitory-to-excitatory weights follow the same symmetric rule with $M>0$, and only first-order motif contributions are included. We assume no additional inhibitory-to-inhibitory connections. This is a generalization of the averaged plasticity equations in @eq-weight-dynamics within that approximation.

### Two effective inhibitory weights {#sec-nk-weight-dynamics}

Under the assumed symmetry within each group, let $W_c$ be the common inhibitory-to-excitatory weight of the $K$ neurons receiving the excitatory connection, and $W_u$ the common weight of the remaining $N-K$ neurons. The subscripts $c$ and $u$ denote neurons with and without that direct excitatory connection. The two effective weights obey

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_e&=h_e-r_i\,\left[K\,W_c+(N-K)\,W_u\right], \\
\frac{d\,W_c}{dt}
&=\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i
 +\left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i+M\,W_e\right)\,r_e
 -M\,r_i\,W_c, \\
\frac{d\,W_u}{dt}
&=\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i
 +\left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i\right)\,r_e
 -M\,r_i\,W_u.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-group-dynamics}

These equations preserve equal weights within each group. The weight $W_c$ is a weight per synapse; the targeted group's total inhibitory weight is $K\,W_c$, and the untargeted group's is $(N-K)\,W_u$.

Define the total weight and the difference between the two effective weights as

$$
W_s:=K\,W_c+(N-K)\,W_u,
\qquad
W_d:=W_c-W_u.
$$ {#eq-nk-mode-definitions}

The inverse transformation is

$$
W_c=\frac{W_s+(N-K)\,W_d}{N},
\qquad
W_u=\frac{W_s-K\,W_d}{N}.
$$ {#eq-nk-mode-inverse}

### Closed sum and difference equations {#sec-nk-mode-dynamics}

Multiplying the two equations in @eq-nk-group-dynamics by their group sizes and adding, or subtracting them directly, yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_e&=h_e-r_i\,W_s, \\
\frac{d\,W_s}{dt}
&=N\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i
 +\left(N\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+N\,B\,r_i+K\,M\,W_e\right)\,r_e
 -M\,r_i\,W_s, \\
\frac{d\,W_d}{dt}
&=-M\,r_i\,W_d+M\,W_e\,r_e.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-mode-dynamics}

Only the sum equation acquires the population factors $N$ and $K$. The shared plasticity terms still cancel from the difference of effective weights. The excitatory contribution to that difference is $M\,W_e\,r_e$ because each targeted neuron receives one synapse of weight $W_e$.

Define the generalized coefficients

$$
\begin{aligned}
c_1^{(N,K)}&:=N\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+N\,B\,r_i+K\,M\,W_e, \\
c_2^{(N,K)}&:=c_1^{(N,K)}+M
 =M\,(1+K\,W_e)+N\,\alpha_{\text{post}}+N\,B\,r_i.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-coefficients}

The closed equations are then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\,W_s}{dt}
&=N\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i+c_1^{(N,K)}\,h_e
 -r_i\,c_2^{(N,K)}\,W_s, \\
\frac{d\,W_d}{dt}
&=-M\,r_i\,W_d+M\,W_e\,\left(h_e-r_i\,W_s\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-closed-dynamics}

### Fixed points and admissibility {#sec-nk-fixed-points}

For $c_2^{(N,K)}\ne0$, the algebraic fixed point is

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&=\frac{M\,h_e-N\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i}{c_2^{(N,K)}}, \\
W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&=\frac{h_e-r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{r_i}
 =\frac{N\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i+c_1^{(N,K)}\,h_e}
 {r_i\,c_2^{(N,K)}}, \\
W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&=\frac{W_e\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{r_i}, \\
W_c^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&=\frac{h_e+\left[(N-K)\,W_e-1\right]\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{N\,r_i} \\
&=\frac{\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,\left[1-(N-K)\,W_e\right]\,r_i
 +\left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i+M\,W_e\right)\,h_e}
 {r_i\,c_2^{(N,K)}}, \\
W_u^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}
&=\frac{h_e-(1+K\,W_e)\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{N\,r_i} \\
&=\frac{\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,(1+K\,W_e)\,r_i
 +\left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i\right)\,h_e}
 {r_i\,c_2^{(N,K)}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-fixed-points}

For $W_e>0$ and $r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}>0$, each targeted synapse is stronger than each untargeted synapse.

For $W_e\ge0$, nonnegative weights and excitatory rate at the fixed point are equivalent to

$$
0\le r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}\le\frac{h_e}{1+K\,W_e}.
$$ {#eq-nk-admissibility}

Indeed, the upper bound is the condition $W_u^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}\ge0$, and $W_c^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}=W_u^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}+W_e\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}/r_i\ge0$ then follows. Strictly positive rates and weights require strict inequalities. These are fixed-point conditions; they do not impose clipping or ensure that every unconstrained trajectory stays in the nonnegative domain.

#### Difference relative to the total weight {#sec-nk-mode-ratio}

For $W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}>0$ and $r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}>0$,

$$
\frac{W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}
=\frac{W_e\,r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{h_e-r_e^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}.
$$ {#eq-nk-difference-sum-ratio}

Since $W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}-K\,W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}=N\,W_u^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$, a useful normalized contrast is

$$
\rho_{N,K}:=\frac{K\,W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}
=\frac{K\,W_e\,\left(M\,h_e-N\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i\right)}
 {N\,\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,r_i+c_1^{(N,K)}\,h_e}.
$$ {#eq-nk-normalized-contrast}

For $W_e>0$ and a fixed point with strictly positive rates and weights, $0<\rho_{N,K}<1$, or equivalently $0<W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}/W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}<1/K$. The boundary $\rho_{N,K}=1$ means all untargeted weights vanish. For a stable algebraic fixed point, this boundary and its continuation to negative untargeted weights are determined by

$$
W_u^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}<0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\alpha_{\text{pre}}\,(1+K\,W_e)\,r_i
 +\left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i\right)\,h_e<0.
$$ {#eq-nk-untargeted-negative}

The fraction of total inhibitory weight carried by the targeted group is

$$
\frac{K\,W_c^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}{W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}}
=\frac{K}{N}+\frac{N-K}{N}\,\rho_{N,K}.
$$ {#eq-nk-targeted-weight-fraction}

Thus equal weights give a targeted share $K/N$, while $\rho_{N,K}\to1$ concentrates the total weight in the targeted group.

### Convergence timescales of the two effective weights {#sec-nk-timescales}

Writing $\delta W_s:=W_s-W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$ and $\delta W_d:=W_d-W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$, the two-mode system satisfies

$$
\frac{d}{dt}
\begin{pmatrix}\delta W_s\\\delta W_d\end{pmatrix}
=
\eta\,
\begin{pmatrix}
-r_i\,c_2^{(N,K)}&0\\
-M\,W_e\,r_i&-M\,r_i
\end{pmatrix}
\,\begin{pmatrix}\delta W_s\\\delta W_d\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-nk-mode-deviations}

Its two eigenvalues are

$$
\lambda_s=-\eta\,r_i\,c_2^{(N,K)},
\qquad
\lambda_d=-\eta\,M\,r_i.
$$ {#eq-nk-eigenvalues}

Since $M>0$ and $r_i>0$, the unconstrained fixed point is asymptotically stable precisely when $c_2^{(N,K)}>0$. The timescales and their ratio are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_s^{(N,K)}&=\frac{1}{\eta\,r_i\,c_2^{(N,K)}},
&\tau_d^{(N,K)}&=\frac{1}{\eta\,M\,r_i}, \\
\frac{\tau_d^{(N,K)}}{\tau_s^{(N,K)}}
&=1+K\,W_e+\frac{N\,\left(\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i\right)}{M}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-timescales}

The sum is much faster when this ratio is much larger than one. Increasing $K$ at fixed weight per excitatory synapse strengthens the total feedback contribution $K\,W_e$; increasing $N$ scales the shared postsynaptic and rate-dependent terms. Neither changes the intrinsic difference timescale when $M$ and $r_i$ are fixed. The difference is forced by the sum and generally contains both timescales. If $c_2^{(N,K)}=M$, this forcing can produce a $t\,e^{-\eta\,M\,r_i\,t}$ transient, as in the three-neuron case.

### Target-rate calibration and rule comparison for general N and K {#sec-nk-rule-comparison}

Setting @eq-nk-fixed-points equal to the target rate gives

$$
\alpha_{\text{pre}}
=-\frac{\alpha_{\text{post}}+B\,r_i}{r_i}\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}
+\frac{M}{N\,r_i}\,[h_e-(1+K\,W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}].
$$ {#eq-nk-target-calibration}

With this calibration, the final weights in @eq-nk-fixed-points depend on the rule only through the common target rate. Strictly positive weights and rate require $0<r_e^{\text{(target)}}<h_e/(1+K\,W_e)$.

For the report's choices $\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{Vog}}=\alpha_{\text{post}}^{\text{cov}}=0$, $B^{\text{Vog}}=1$, and $B^{\text{cov}}=0$, the calibrated constants are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{Vog}}
&=-r_e^{\text{(target)}}+\frac{M^{\text{Vog}}}{N\,r_i}\,[h_e-(1+K\,W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}],\\
\alpha_{\text{pre}}^{\text{cov}}
&=\frac{M^{\text{cov}}}{N\,r_i}\,[h_e-(1+K\,W_e)\,r_e^{\text{(target)}}].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-rule-calibration}

Including the rule-specific learning rates, the timescales are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_s^{(N,K),\text{Vog}}&=\frac{1}{\eta^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i\,[M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+K\,W_e)+N\,r_i]},
&\tau_d^{(N,K),\text{Vog}}&=\frac{1}{\eta^{\text{Vog}}\,M^{\text{Vog}}\,r_i},\\
\tau_s^{(N,K),\text{cov}}&=\frac{1}{\eta^{\text{cov}}\,M^{\text{cov}}\,r_i\,(1+K\,W_e)},
&\tau_d^{(N,K),\text{cov}}&=\frac{1}{\eta^{\text{cov}}\,M^{\text{cov}}\,r_i}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-nk-rule-timescales}

The difference-to-sum timescale ratios are $1+K\,W_e+N\,r_i/M^{\text{Vog}}$ and $1+K\,W_e$, respectively. Matching the sum timescales requires

$$
\frac{\eta^{\text{Vog}}}{\eta^{\text{cov}}}
=\frac{M^{\text{cov}}\,(1+K\,W_e)}{M^{\text{Vog}}\,(1+K\,W_e)+N\,r_i}.
$$ {#eq-nk-matched-learning-rates}

For general postsynaptic constants, replace the numerator and denominator by each rule's $c_2^{(N,K)}$ from @eq-nk-coefficients. With nonnegative shared postsynaptic and rate-dependent contributions, the sum is at least as fast as the difference.

### Recovery of the three-neuron case {#sec-nk-three-neuron-recovery}

Setting $N=2$ and $K=1$ gives $W_c=W_1$, $W_u=W_2$, $W_s=W_1+W_2$, and $W_d=W_1-W_2$. The generalized coefficients become $c_1$ and $c_2$ from @eq-mode-coefficients, and @eq-nk-mode-dynamics, @eq-nk-fixed-points, and @eq-nk-timescales reduce to the previous dynamics, fixed points, and timescales. The normalized contrast becomes $\rho_{2,1}=W_d^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}/W_s^{\left( t \rightarrow \infty \right)}$.

## Conclusions

At a common calibrated target rate, the stable fixed point is rule-invariant. In the small-motif regime, the Vogels sum mode relaxes much faster than its difference mode. For the covariance rule with zero postsynaptic constant and $W_e$ of order one, the two timescales are comparable. Matching the sum timescales therefore gives faster weight separation under the covariance rule, as illustrated by the supplied simulations. Both rules still have a difference mode slower than their sum mode.

The report raises the possibility that finite simulation durations can mask slow weight adaptation in existing work. This is an interpretation to investigate; establishing it for another model requires that model's parameters and convergence analysis.

The report includes the following panel from [Lagzi & Fairhall (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adi4350) as motivation for that comparison. The panel alone does not establish whether the simulation reached its asymptotic weights.
